analysis.one_liner: Directed federal regulators to cap western wholesale electricity prices at cost-based levels during the power crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill, written amid the 2000–01 western power crisis, drew bipartisan cosponsors and a Senate hearing but never got a committee vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000–2001 western electricity crisis, when spot power prices in California and neighboring states hit many times their old levels, this bill would have ordered the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to impose cost-based wholesale rates across the western energy market within 60 days. It also let state regulators block utilities from selling power out of state when local supply was at risk, required natural gas sellers shipping into California to disclose what portion of their price was the gas versus the pipeline transportation, and urged the Bonneville Power Administration to limit a coming rate increase. It got a Senate hearing in June 2001 but never came up for a vote, and expired at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses across the western energy market — most of all in California — who were paying crisis-level wholesale power prices passed through to retail bills. State utility regulators would have gained new authority to keep power inside their states during shortages.

how_it_helps.text: Would have required FERC to impose just-and-reasonable, cost-based wholesale rates on public utilities in the western energy market within 60 days of enactment, replacing spot prices that the bill's findings said were 'multiples' of pre-2000 levels [S3].

Would have let state public utility commissions bar utilities under their authority from selling power to out-of-state buyers when that delivery could impair in-state supply — a direct response to California's supply crunch [S2] [S3].

Would have required natural gas sellers shipping into California to disclose separately the commodity and transportation portions of bundled sale prices, addressing gas prices that the bill's findings said were feeding into electricity costs [S2] [S3].
Would have expressed the Senate's view that the Bonneville Power Administration should cut its wholesale power purchases and minimize a rate increase set to take effect October 1, 2001 [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers — generators and utilities charging crisis-level spot prices — would have lost that premium revenue and been limited to production costs plus a reasonable return. Gas sellers into California would have faced new price-disclosure paperwork. The bill's carve-outs also barred federal orders forcing sellers to deliver power or gas to states (in practice, California) without reasonable assurance of payment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale power sellers and gas marketers

drawbacks.text: Cost-based rate caps on wholesale power during a genuine supply shortage drew the standard objection that they would discourage investment in new generation precisely when more supply was needed — the reason many economists prefer market prices even in a crisis [S3].

The bill itself was hedged: the rate mandate would not apply in states with retail price limits that precluded sellers from being paid on time, and sellers could not be ordered to deliver power or gas into such a state without reasonable assurance of payment — provisions aimed squarely at California's payment problems that diluted the protection buyers would get [S3].
The rate mandate was temporary: the whole section would have repealed itself effective March 1, 2003, leaving the underlying market structure unchanged [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For western consumers facing prices many times the pre-2000 level, the benefit of cost-based rates would likely have outweighed the cost, and the sunset and payment-assurance carve-outs limited the risk to sellers. The strongest honest objection is that caps during a shortage can delay new supply; the bill's carve-outs and short sunset were designed to blunt that criticism, making it a relatively cautious intervention rather than a sweeping price freeze.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held one hearing in June 2001 but never voted it out, so the full Senate never considered it and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 24, 2001 by Sen. Feinstein with six cosponsors including Sen. Gordon Smith (R-OR), Sen. Bingaman (D-NM), Sens. Murray and Cantwell (D-WA), and Sen. Lieberman (I/D-CT), and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1] [S4] [S5].
The committee held a hearing on June 19, 2001 (S.Hrg. 107-183) — the only action after referral [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale power sellers were better off because the bill died: no cost-based rate cap was imposed by Congress, and they continued selling under whatever federal mitigation FERC chose to apply rather than a statutory cost-of-service ceiling.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers charging crisis prices

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S5].

for.name: Sen. Gordon Smith of Oregon and five other senators
for.role: Cosponsors (5 of 49 Senate Democrats, 1 of 49 Senate Republicans, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan western support [S4].

for.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on June 19, 2001; took no further action [S5].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (majority-controlled by Democrats in 2001)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out after its hearing, keeping it from the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed broad federal wholesale price caps during the California crisis, arguing they would worsen shortages, and resisted congressional pressure for them.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan (5 of 49 Senate Democrats, 1 of 49 Senate Republicans, plus 1 Independent), and no recorded vote ever showed how the chambers would have split; opposition never appeared in a roll call.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers (generators and utilities trading in western spot markets)
industries.note: The bill would have replaced crisis spot prices — which the bill's own findings said ran at multiples of pre-2000 levels — with cost-of-service rates capped at costs plus a reasonable return. Ordinary western ratepayers paid those spot prices at retail, so the industry's gain ran directly against the public's cost.

industries.industry: Natural gas sellers and pipeline companies shipping gas into California
industries.note: They would have lost the ability to keep bundled commodity and transportation charges opaque and faced new disclosure rules, though no rate cap. The provision targeted the high gas prices feeding into California electricity costs.

industries.industry: Western public utilities and state utility regulators
industries.note: Utilities buying wholesale power would have paid less, while sellers among them would have earned less; state regulators gained explicit authority to block exports during shortages and to keep control over how wholesale rates pass through to retail customers.
A Senate-expressed view urged it to cut power purchases and minimize an October 2001 rate increase — a cost message to a federal power marketer whose rates flow to Northwest consumers.
